headline: The History of Photography - Origin of Photography to Today

description: The history of photography, from early camera obscura to AI-powered digital imaging. Explore key milestones from the origin of photography to modern photography.
articleBody: The History of Photography - Origin of Photography to Today Updated 15 Oct 2026 Table of Contents Show The History of Photography: A Journey Through Time Photography has transformed the way we see and document the world. From early light projections to the digital revolution, the history of photography showcases human ingenuity and artistic expression. Understanding its evolution offers insight into the technology shaping modern imaging. The Birth of Photography: The camera obscura was known in antiquity and later used by artists to study and draw scenes. In the 1820 s, Joseph Nicéphore Niépce made the earliest surviving permanent camera photograph using a light-sensitive bitumen coating. Daguerre’s process was announced in 1839; Talbot’s calotype, patented in 1841, made multiple prints from a paper negative possible. Technological Advances: Archer’s wet collodion process (1851) produced detailed negatives but had to be prepared and developed while wet. Eastman’s Kodak camera (1888) brought simple roll-film photography to more people. The Leica I helped popularise 35mm cameras in 1925; Kodachrome followed in 1935. Polaroid demonstrated instant photography in 1947 and sold its first Land Camera in 1948. The Digital Age and AI: Kodak engineer Steven Sasson built a digital camera prototype in 1975. Digital cameras later became widely used, followed by camera phones and smartphones. Computational photography combines or processes multiple captures; generative AI can also create images that were never photographed. These are related technologies, but they are not the same thing. Why Photography’s History Matters: Each milestone changed how images could be made, copied, shared or interpreted. Understanding that history helps us see what technology contributes—and what still depends on the photographer’s choices. Want to put what you have learned into practice? Centuries later, the camera obscura became a practical optical device for projecting a scene. It could display an image, but could not preserve it as a photograph. What changed — and what came next?01Why did this matter? A projected image could be studied, but not kept. 02How was it used, and what did it make possible? The camera obscura helped artists and observers inspect a scene. 03What pushed photography forward next? The next step was to use projection as a practical drawing aid. By the 16th century, camera obscura devices were being described as aids for drawing. They projected a scene onto a surface, where an artist could study or trace its forms. The projection itself was temporary; it did not record a photograph. The camera obscura turned an optical effect into a working tool. Artists used the projection to study form and perspective. The remaining problem was preserving the projected image. 19th Century: The Birth of Photography Niépce’s View from the Window at Le Gras, made around 1826–1827, is the earliest surviving photograph made with a camera. He used a light-sensitive bitumen coating on a metal plate and a very long exposure. The image is faint and difficult to interpret, but it permanently recorded a view. Joseph Nicéphore Niépce, View from the Window at Le Gras, c. 1826–1827. The earliest surviving photograph made with a camera.What changed — and what came next?01Why did this matter? Niépce proved that a camera could make a lasting record. Heliography exposed a bitumen-coated plate for many hours. The next processes sought clearer detail and more usable photographs. Daguerre’s process was announced publicly in 1839. A daguerreotype was a unique image on a silver-coated copper plate, not a negative from which prints could be made. It could show exceptionally fine detail, though the image needed careful viewing and protection. Illustration of Louis Daguerre demonstrating the daguerreotype process.What changed — and what came next?01Why did this matter? Photography became public and could show remarkable detail. Photographers made portraits on unique polished plates. The need for repeatable copies encouraged negative-positive methods. Talbot’s calotype used a paper negative to make multiple positive prints. Its images were generally less sharply defined than daguerreotypes, but the negative-positive method became a foundation for later photographic printing. One negative could produce multiple positive prints. Talbot used paper negatives to make repeatable copies. The search for sharper detail led to glass-plate processes. Frederick Scott Archer published the wet collodion process in 1851. It could produce detailed glass-plate negatives and shorter exposures than earlier paper-negative methods, but each plate had to be coated, exposed and developed before it dried. Glass negatives improved detail and shortened exposures. Each plate had to be prepared, exposed and developed while wet. The burden of wet plates created demand for easier roll-film cameras. Eastman’s Kodak camera, launched in 1888, came preloaded with roll film. Customers returned the camera to Kodak for processing and reloading, making photography simpler for non-specialists. The key change was access and convenience, not a direct image-quality comparison with later compact cameras. Roll film and processing services widened access to photography. Customers returned the camera to Kodak for processing and reloading. X-ray imaging showed photography could record beyond visible light. In 1895, Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen discovered X-rays and made radiographs that showed structures hidden beneath the skin. His image of his wife’s hand became an early, famous demonstration. X-ray imaging expanded photography’s use beyond visible light into medicine and science. Radiography extended image-making into medicine and science. X-rays revealed structures hidden beneath the skin. Commercial colour processes changed what photographs could show. Autochrome made colour photographs by using microscopic dyed starch grains on a glass plate. It produced distinctive, often soft-looking transparencies and was an important early commercial colour process; it was not the first attempt to make colour photographs. Autochrome brought colour photography into commercial use. Photographers recorded colour on glass plates using dyed starch grains. The next major shift made cameras more portable. 20th Century: The Rise of Modern Photography The Leica I, introduced in 1925, helped establish the compact 35mm camera as a practical tool. Its small negative required precise lenses and enlargement, and its influence came from portability and a usable system—not from replacing every larger-format camera. A compact 35mm camera made photography easier to carry. Photographers exposed a small negative and enlarged it later. Colour film made colour photography more practical. Introduced in 1935, Kodachrome was an important colour reversal film known for rich colour and fine detail when properly exposed and processed. It was one of several developments that made colour photography more practical. Colour reversal film produced vivid transparencies. Kodachrome depended on careful exposure and processing. Instant photography promised a finished print without a lab wait. Land’s system produced a finished photograph within minutes, without sending film away for processing. Early models used a peel-apart process; later instant films integrated the image and processing materials. It made immediate prints practical, rather than matching the quality or process of an inkjet print. A finished photograph could be available within minutes. Early Polaroid cameras used peel-apart materials; later films integrated the process. Computers would soon store photographic information as digital data. Kirsch’s 1957 scan measured 176 × 176 pixels. It was a digital image made by scanning a photograph, not a photograph captured by a digital camera. The distinction matters: digital capture came later. A scanned photograph could be represented as pixels. Kirsch’s team digitised a physical image; this was not camera capture. Camera makers made film cameras simpler for a mass audience. Introduced in 1963, Kodak’s Instamatic cameras used easy-to-load film cartridges and simple controls. They helped make casual photography more convenient; the comparison with smartphone cameras is about ease of use, not equivalent technology or image quality. Easy loading and simple controls widened casual photography. Instamatic cartridges removed the need to handle loose film. Digital sensors would replace film as the recording medium. In 1975, Kodak engineer Steven Sasson built an experimental self-contained digital camera using a CCD sensor. It recorded a black-and-white image of about 100 × 100 pixels to a cassette tape and took roughly 23 seconds to capture it. This was a laboratory prototype, not a consumer camera. A sensor could capture an image directly as digital data. Sasson’s prototype recorded a small black-and-white image to tape. Electronic still cameras explored alternatives to film. The 1981 Mavica was a prototype, not a released digital camera. Its analogue electronic recording was an alternative to film; later Mavica models reached consumers. It should not be described as digitally storing images or assigned a digital-camera megapixel rating. Electronic image capture could be explored without digital files. The Mavica prototype recorded analogue video signals to magnetic disk. Autofocus and electronic lens communication reshaped SLR cameras. Canon launched the EOS autofocus SLR system in 1987. It introduced electronic communication between camera and lens and a new lens mount. These were film SLRs; digital SLRs arrived later. The camera and lens could communicate electronically for autofocus. Canon’s EOS system introduced a new mount on film SLRs. Digital capture moved into professional work with the Kodak DCS 100. Introduced in 1991, the Kodak DCS 100 combined a Nikon F-3 film SLR body with a digital imaging system and external storage unit. Its 1.3-megapixel sensor made it a landmark professional digital camera, though it was large and very expensive. Digital capture reached professional assignments despite high cost and bulk. The DCS 100 paired a Nikon film body with digital hardware and storage. Phones would make cameras part of everyday communication. 21st Century: The Digital Revolution & AI Photography The J-SH04 helped popularise a built-in camera phone in Japan. Its camera produced small, low-resolution images, but it was not the first commercial camera phone: Kyocera’s VP-210 had appeared the previous year. The camera became part of a device people carried everywhere. Camera phones made quick images easier to capture and . Digital camera sales soon overtook film in major markets. The transition happened over several years and varied by market. Megapixels alone are not a fair way to compare digital cameras with film: film has no fixed pixel count, and results depend on film, lens, exposure, scanning or printing, and viewing size. Digital capture changed storage, review and copying at scale. The transition took years; film production did not end at once. Connected smartphones made images easier to edit and . Apple’s first iPhone, released in 2007, had a 2-megapixel rear camera. Camera phones already existed; the iPhone’s significance was its role in the evolution of the smartphone as a connected camera, alongside the touchscreen and software ecosystem. The camera became part of a connected software platform. The first iPhone combined capture with a touchscreen and internet access. Mirrorless systems offered compact bodies with interchangeable lenses. Mirrorless cameras remove the reflex mirror used in DSLRs and can use sensors comparable in size to those in DSLRs. The Sony NEX-7 showed that a compact body could offer a 24-megapixel APS-C sensor and interchangeable lenses; its results still depended on lens, exposure and use. Compact mirrorless bodies could use large sensors and interchangeable lenses. The NEX-7 paired an APS-C sensor with a compact camera body. Multi-frame processing could improve what a single exposure recorded. HDR+ combines multiple exposures and aligns and merges them to control highlights, reduce noise and preserve detail. It is computational photography; calling the original HDR+ system “AI-powered” overstates what the technique was. Software could combine captures to control highlights and noise. HDR+ aligned and merged short exposures; it is computational photography. Generative systems began making images without photographing a scene. Generative systems can create or alter images without photographing the depicted scene. Their growing public visibility accelerated from 2022, though the underlying research is older. These synthetic images raise questions about authorship, evidence and disclosure; they are distinct from photographs made with a camera. Images could be generated without photographing the depicted scene. Generative systems raised questions about authorship, evidence and disclosure. The next debate is how audiences distinguish photographs from synthetic images. Smartphone sensors are physically much smaller than those in most DSLR and mirrorless cameras. Software can combine exposures, reduce noise and sharpen detail, but it cannot enlarge the sensor or give it the same physical light-gathering capacity. The best result depends on the subject and conditions. Read my guide to full-frame versus cropped sensors to understand how sensor size affects image quality. Camera choice depends on the physical and computational strengths needed. Phones work well in many situations; larger sensors and lenses offer different options. Future changes will keep testing the balance between sensor, software and judgement. Photography has evolved from early optical projections and the first permanent photographs to digital capture and image processing. Each milestone changed how images could be made, copied, shared or interpreted. From Niépce’s heliograph to computational smartphone photography, the story includes both technical change and new ways for people to use images. As I explore in my article “Beyond a Point-and-Shoot Camera”, choosing a camera depends on the subject, conditions and result you want. Phones can make excellent pictures in many everyday situations. DSLR and mirrorless cameras offer larger sensors, interchangeable lenses and direct controls, which can be important for low light, depth of field, action or particular ways of working. Photography will keep changing as cameras and software develop. Whether you use a phone, compact, DSLR or mirrorless camera, stronger photographs still begin with noticing light, making considered choices and using your equipment with purpose.
